content.title: Zeros, Vertex, and Axis of Symmetry of a Quadratic
content.overview: This lesson covers the essential features of a quadratic function in standard form (ax² + bx + c). You will learn to calculate the axis of symmetry, locate the vertex, and identify the zeros (roots) of the parabola using algebraic formulas and verification techniques.
learning_objectives: Calculate the axis of symmetry using the formula x = -b/(2a).
Determine the vertex coordinates by evaluating the function at the axis of symmetry.
Identify the zeros of a quadratic function through factoring or the quadratic formula.
Verify the relationship between the zeros and the axis of symmetry.

sections.title: The Axis of Symmetry
sections.content: The axis of symmetry is a vertical line that divides a parabola into two congruent halves. For any quadratic function in the standard form f(x) = ax² + bx + c, the equation for the axis of symmetry is x = -b/(2a). This line always passes through the vertex of the parabola.

sections.title: Locating the Vertex
sections.content:
The vertex is the highest (maximum) or lowest (minimum) point on a parabola. The x-coordinate of the vertex is always the same value as the axis of symmetry. To find the y-coordinate of the vertex, substitute the x-value back into the original quadratic equation: y = f(-b/(2a)). The vertex is expressed as the ordered pair (x, y).

![A flow chart showing the steps to find quadratic features: Calculate Axis, Find Vertex, Find Zeros, and Verify Midpoint.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/771066e6-f336-4e6f-9dd2-f260d545a201-1786505685484-108.webp)

sections.title: Finding the Zeros
sections.content: The zeros (also called roots or x-intercepts) are the x-values where the graph crosses the x-axis, meaning f(x) = 0. You can find these by factoring the quadratic expression or by using the quadratic formula. A key property of parabolas is that the axis of symmetry is always the midpoint (average) of the two zeros: Axis x = (Zero1 + Zero2) / 2.

worked_examples.question: Given the function f(x) = 2x² - 8x + 6, identify the axis of symmetry, the vertex, and the zeros.
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Find the axis of symmetry using x = -b/(2a). Here, a = 2 and b = -8. So, x = -(-8) / (2 * 2) = 8 / 4 = 2. The axis is x = 2.
Step 2: Find the vertex y-coordinate by plugging x = 2 into the function. f(2) = 2(2)² - 8(2) + 6 = 2(4) - 16 + 6 = 8 - 16 + 6 = -2. The vertex is (2, -2).
Step 3: Find the zeros by setting f(x) = 0. 2x² - 8x + 6 = 0. Divide by 2: x² - 4x + 3 = 0. Factor: (x - 1)(x - 3) = 0. The zeros are x = 1 and x = 3.
Step 4: Verify. The average of the zeros is (1 + 3) / 2 = 2, which matches our axis of symmetry.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the negative sign in the axis formula: using x = b/(2a) instead of x = -b/(2a).
Confusing the x and y coordinates of the vertex.
Assuming a quadratic always has two real zeros; some may have one or none.
Incorrectly identifying 'b' when the quadratic is not in standard order (e.g., c + ax² + bx).
exam_tips: If you find the zeros first, simply average them to find the x-coordinate of the vertex.
Always check the sign of 'a'. If 'a' is positive, the vertex is a minimum; if 'a' is negative, the vertex is a maximum.
Use the 'Vertex-Axis-Zero Fast Check': the axis must be exactly halfway between the zeros.
content.recap: To analyze a quadratic f(x) = ax² + bx + c, calculate the axis of symmetry with x = -b/(2a). This x-value is the vertex's x-coordinate; plug it in to find y. The zeros are the solutions to f(x) = 0, and their midpoint must align with the axis of symmetry.

knowledge_claims.content: The axis of symmetry for a quadratic in the form ax² + bx + c is defined by the vertical line equation x = -b/(2a).
The vertex of a parabola is the point where the graph changes direction, representing either the maximum or minimum value of the function.
To find the y-coordinate of the vertex, substitute the x-coordinate (found via the axis of symmetry formula) into the original quadratic equation.
Zeros of a quadratic function are the x-values where the function equals zero, corresponding to the x-intercepts on a graph.
The axis of symmetry is always located at the midpoint (arithmetic mean) of the two zeros of a quadratic function.
A valid check for the vertex x-coordinate is to verify that it equals (Zero1 + Zero2) / 2.
If the coefficient 'a' in ax² + bx + c is positive, the parabola opens upward and the vertex is a minimum point.
If the coefficient 'a' in ax² + bx + c is negative, the parabola opens downward and the vertex is a maximum point.
A common error is failing to apply the negative sign to the 'b' value when calculating the axis of symmetry x = -b/(2a).
The x-coordinate of the vertex and the value of the axis of symmetry are always identical.
Factoring the quadratic expression ax² + bx + c = 0 is a primary method for identifying the zeros of the function.
When a quadratic is not easily factorable, the quadratic formula can be used to find the zeros before averaging them to find the axis.
